outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN), and file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the County Clerk if the public-facing name differs from the legal entity name. What to say: Register online at sftreasurer.org; the BAN is issued within 1–5 days. The registration fee is tiered by gross receipts (e.g. $55 for under $100k, $95 for $100k–$250k, plus a $4 state fee). outcomes.original: Filing step: File a Conditional Use Authorization application with San Francisco Planning, including a pre-application meeting with the Zoning Administrator, community outreach, and 300-foot property owner notification. What to say: Email the Planning Department's front desk to schedule a pre-application meeting to confirm the CUA pathway and fee (likely $3,100 base fee for no construction, CPI-adjusted each July, or higher if construction cost is stated). At the meeting, describe the concept as a beer-and-wine bar (Type 42) with limited food service, confirm that it is not part of a chain (if true), and state the floor area. After the meeting, submit the CUA application with site plans, a project description emphasizing the food component and neighborhood fit, and a Good Neighbor Policy addressing noise, litter, and patron management. Planning will post a yellow notice at the site for 30 days, mail notice to property owners within 300 feet, and schedule a Planning Commission hearing. The hearing is typically 4–6 months after filing; the CUA must be approved before ABC or DBI will act.
outcomes.note: Records confirm CUA process, 300-foot notice, hearing, and fee range, but don't describe pre-application meeting procedure, notice color/duration, July CPI adjustment, or ABC/DBI prerequisite.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for an ABC Type 42 license (on-sale beer and wine, public premises) with the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, or arrange to transfer an existing Type 42 license to this location. What to say: File the application online at abc.ca.gov with the signed lease, seller's permit, entity documents, seller's permit, and a $1,000–$1,600 filing fee. Post a 30-day public notice at the premises. ABC will automatically refer the application to San Francisco Planning and the Police Department for review under Business and Professions Code Section 23987; wait for Planning's CUA approval before expecting ABC to issue. If the census tract is over-concentrated (tract 117.00 shows 89 on-sale licenses against 6 authorized), ABC may require a Public Convenience or Necessity finding from the Board of Supervisors; coordinate with Planning to obtain the PCN letter as part of the CUA process. Type 42 is non-quota (ABC issues new ones), but city approval is the long pole. Budget 60–150 days from ABC application to issuance if unprotested, longer if a PCN hearing is needed.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit a health permit application (and plan check if kitchen work is involved) to the San Francisco Department of Public Health Environmental Health Branch, with the BAN, food safety manager certificate, and menu. What to say: Apply online at sfdph.org/ehsportal at least one month before opening. The $470 permit application includes the initial inspection; the annual license fee is $0 for bars and restaurants through 2028 under the FY2026–27 fee schedule. If you are installing or modifying a kitchen, submit a plan check application ($828–$2,207 depending on scope) with scaled drawings, equipment specs, finishes, and the menu; DPH will route it to DBI for the building permit. After approval, schedule a pre-final inspection at ~80% construction complete and a final inspection at least two weeks before opening. You must have a certified food safety manager on staff (ServSafe or equivalent, $100–$250, valid 5 years) and every employee who handles food must obtain a California Food Handler Card ($7–$15, valid 3 years) within 30 days of hire.

What to say: Submit the application at sfdbi.org/permit-application after the CUA is approved. The application will be routed to Planning, which will attach the CUA as a condition. Schedule the final DBI inspection, the DPH final inspection, and any Fire Department inspection in sequence; DPH will not issue the permit to operate until DBI signs off.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $4,795 to $18,920. Notes: The day and cost ranges cover obtaining the approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000 depending on construction cost), Health permit to operate (14–45 days, $470–$1,000), and Building permit with change of use (14–120 days, $800–$15,000 depending on scope). These are times to approval. The CUA is the critical path: 4–10 months including pre-application, community outreach, environmental review, hearing scheduling, and the 30-day appeal period. The ABC Type 42 application (60–150 days, $1,000–$1,600) runs in parallel after the CUA is filed but cannot be issued until the CUA is approved, so it does not add time to the path. Additional state and city registration fees (business registration $55–$700, entity formation $70–$150, seller's permit $0, FBN $60–$120, sign permit $300–$1,500, music licenses $600–$5,000/year) and one-time costs (food safety certifications $107–$265, RBS training ~$50 for a small staff) bring the low-end total to roughly $6,500–$7,500 in government fees and the high-end to $20,000–$25,000 if construction triggers higher permit fees and a large CUA application fee. These figures exclude lease costs, construction, inventory, insurance, and attorney or consultant fees.
